utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today's Thursday. A very good morning to all of you. We are starting a bit late because there's this recurrent and very familiar technical problem which is still with us. The technician has told us that he is unable to identify the cause of the problem, because apparently this is a problem that lies only with Courtroom III. It doesn't exist elsewhere. It's only connected with our courtroom, but they cannot manage to find the cause in spite of all of the efforts they've made. And as was explained by Mr. Khan, quite rightly so yesterday, the system was changed, and that may be the reason for the problem. Whatever the case may be, they've booted up the system, and for the time being it's working. Let's hope it keeps working throughout the morning. You may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor, with your closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel. May it please the Court, I'll be presenting the closing submissions on behalf of the Prosecution in regard to the Accused Valentin Coric. I'd like to begin my remarks by going straight to the two core arguments forming the foundation of the Coric brief and indeed the Coric defence itself. The first of these arguments is a legal one, with Coric asserting that he cannot be held responsible for any of the crimes alleged as a member of a joint criminal enterprise unless he is first found guilty under the principle of command responsibility found in Article 7(3) of the Statute. As he claims in paragraph 150 of his brief, "It's respectfully submitted that it is abundantly clear the OTP cannot succeed in proving a JCE unless the OTP can prove the liability of Coric under Article 7(3) of the Statute." He continues in paragraph 151 of his brief: "Without Article 7(3) liability, there cannot be JCE liability of Coric." The second principle on which Coric bases his defence is, of course, factual. Here Coric hides behind his desk, claiming he was a mere bureaucrat or administrator with no real powers to punish or prevent crimes, no effective control over persons committing the crimes, and as a result, Mr. Coric claims that he didn't really know about crimes that were taking place since communications were bad and he only had "limited reporting" available to him even though he was chief of the Military Police Administration. As a result of this, Coric claims he didn't know about any joint criminal enterprise and that he did not contribute to and was not a member of one. Coric's legal claim that liability for crimes as a member of a joint criminal enterprise is somehow dependent on it first being shown that he's guilty for those crimes under Article 7(3) is easily disposed of. The Trial Chamber will note the appeals judgement in the Kvocka case from February 2005. We have it on the screen. Paragraph 104 of that judgement where the Appeals Chamber notes that participation in a joint criminal enterprise pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute and superior responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute are distinct categories of individual criminal responsibility, each with specific legal requirements. Joint criminal enterprise responsibility does not require any showing of superior responsibility. And then in our slide there we make references to additional parts of the Kvocka appeals judgement, paragraph 144, paragraph 383, that stand for that same proposition. The Trial Chamber will note in addition that in the Krajisnik case, for example, the accused was convicted under joint criminal enterprise even though the Trial Chamber concluded that he did not exercise effective control over the forces who participated in the commission of the crimes. That's at paragraph 1121 of the Krajisnik trial judgement. And so this aspect of the Defence case that any liability for joint criminal enterprise is first dependent on a showing of 7(3) liability has no basis or merit whatsoever. In regards to his involvement and contribution to what we call the Herceg-Bosna joint criminal enterprise, our starting principle is that Mr. Coric, like his co-accused, wanted to bring about creation of Herceg-Bosna, an autonomous Croat territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. P08548. This is the publication entitled "They Years of Military Police," containing the contributions of a number of individuals who had been active in the military police of the HVO. In his contribution to that publication, Mr. Coric, writing about the formation of the military police said: "When selecting members of the military police, we took care to recruit honourable people, people committed to the Croatian cause and the homeland, and I think that we were very successful in that selection." Now, of course it's expected and appropriate that one might select and recruit honourable individuals. Mr. President, it's less clear how many Muslims would have been linked or faithful to the idea of the Croatian cause and the Croatian homeland that formed this cornerstone of recruitment in the military police. Croats weren't the only honourable people in Herceg-Bosna. P01788. This is a document that the Trial Chamber will recall from my submissions regarding General Praljak. These are the notes of a meeting held on the 2nd of April, 1993. Mr. President, I'm being told that my trial assistant's computer has crashed, and so we're not going to be in a position to put these documents up in Sanction. We can try to improvise with e-court in the meantime, and for that I think I'm dependent on the registrar. In any event, I'm going to keep going because it's clear that the technology is determined impede our progress on this final day of the Prosecution closing submissions, which is rather unfortunate indeed. P01788 are the minutes of a meeting held with General Praljak, Mr. Coric, others, and the commands of the HVO. The Trial Chamber will recall this document in this meeting from the words of General Praljak reported here where he said that, "We can only fence off what is ours and build our own state there." He was in this meeting talking about the homogenisation of the populations as part of what we say was his vision of Herceg-Bosna. Valentin Coric was present at this meeting, as were other key individuals in the Herceg-Bosna hierarchy, such as Dario Kordic and Ignjac Kostroman, who was the gentleman from Central Bosnia, the Trial Chamber recalls, was advancing the cause of a secession of Herceg-Bosna to Croatia as part of the dream. P06581. Mr. President, these are the minutes of a meeting held at the presidential palace. Mr. Boban, Dr. Prlic, President Tudjman, in November of 1993, the 10th of November, 1993. At this meeting, the discussion was about appointing and approving individuals who would take the key positions as part of the newly established Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the HR HB. In this meeting, Dr. Prlic stated to Dr. Tudjman: "Valentin Coric, who also enjoys general confidence in the army, is now our commander of the military police. By all his attributes, I can even think he would be a good defence minister." And then he goes on. President Tudjman says: "For those two ministries, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior, you must appoint the most forceful and the most authoritative individuals." Prlic replies: "Valentin is, and Coric absolutely is that, yes." Now, in November of 1993, it's impossible that descriptions such as "forceful" and "authoritative" could be assigned to Mr. Coric if indeed up to that point he was not in a position to know everything that had taken place up to that point. Had he not been an effective commander and chief of the military police, he would not have been approved and put forth to be the minister of interior of the newly declared Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. On the issue of contribution, Mr. President, I should say that Coric misstates the applicable standard for contribution to a joint criminal enterprise in his brief. In paragraph 219 of his brief, he claims that he did not substantially contribute to any JCE. This, of course, is not the required showing. Once Mr. Coric is shown to be a member of the JCE, sharing the intent for the commission of the JCE crimes, his contribution to that need only be significant, but perhaps it's not a vital point because in the Prosecution's submission, it's well-established in this case that Mr. Coric has made a quite substantial contribution to the Herceg-Bosna JCE. As with his co-accused, Coric possessed tremendous power, albeit in his own sphere, the sphere of the military police, the tasks, and the competencies of the military police. One way that he contributed to the JCE was in not exercising his power to prohibit, punish, condemn, or even criticise the widespread criminal conduct directed against the Bosnian Muslim population in Herceg-Bosna. A particularly unsettling aspect of Mr. Coric's involvement in this case is that he was the chief military policeman. He was not a policeman for everyone, however, and certainly not for the Bosnian Muslims. The evidence shows that he, like Praljak, was so committed to the Herceg-Bosna enterprise that he was willing to condone and approve crimes contributing to the establishment of Herceg-Bosna. Coric approved or turned a blind eye to crimes linked to his own subordinates in the military police and also did nothing to support the police efforts to take strong measures against other HVO personnel who were committing crimes, particularly when those criminals were useful in HVO combat operations. In other words, identical to General Praljak's command style, the command climate: If they're good soldiers, if they're good fighters, we'll look the other way when they're committing crimes. We see this in P03928, which is a report dated the 3rd of August, 1993, directed to Mr. Coric personally at the Military Police Administration. The writer of this report is complaining about criminal activities of two well-known units, the Vinko Skrobo, formally Mrmak ATG, and the Benko Penavic ATG. He writes that they're responsible for a large share of the crime in the Mostar town area. He says: "Since these two units are listed as parts of the convicts' battalion, they have a special status for unknown reasons." The special status is reflected in the fact that neither the military police nor any other law enforcement organ is taking any action against members of this unit who are committing crimes. He says, referring to his colleague Zvonko Vidovic, that Vidovic had received an order some time ago from the chief of the Military Police Administration that the centre should only register certain acts committed by certain people from these units. Continuing on to the next page: "I would like to point out that the entire personnel of the above-mentioned units, a large part is involved in criminal activities so that a vigorous pursuit action and bringing of the perpetrators of criminal acts to court would probably lead to the break-up of those units." Now, Mr. President, there's been some evidence that what was really happening is they were holding off on taking measures against these units. They were collecting information, and they were going to wait until the right time to step in and take measures to prevent crimes committed by units such as these. However, we know that such an operation, if it was ever intended, certainly never took place. P05563 is a report, again, dated -- directed I should say directly to the chief of the military police, Mr. Coric. This is coming from Mr. Bozo, Stanko Bozic, who was the warden of the Heliodrom detention facility. It's his report for the month of September 1993, dated 2nd of October of that year. He's making reference to a lot of issues here that are of relevance to this case and Mr. Coric's responsibility. The initial section of the report he indicates that on the 9th of September, 351 detainees were transferred from Ljubuski, which had led to the prison being even more overcrowded. The transfer has led to a number of problems. He refers to an order by Mr. Mladen Naletilic Tuta on 21 and -- 20 and 21 September where he says that: "24 of our detainees why released for the requirements of the front line." Mr. President, what the evidence would show is that those were actually not Muslim detainees. Those were, in all likelihood, very hardened Croat criminals, murderers, who were released from the Heliodrom just prior to the HVO operation directed by Mr. Tuta and the Convicts Battalion at Rastani. So the criminals were let out of gaol to go fight for the HVO. It's being reported to Mr. Coric. We don't know. There's certainly no evidence that Mr. Coric or anyone else did anything about this. We do know that Mr. Coric's co-accused, Mr. Stojic, subsequently commended, issued a commendation, to the members of the Convicts Battalion, congratulating for their successful operation at Rastani, an operation that we now know was one in which many crimes were committed. The report goes on. We're going to talk about the forced labour later in my remarks. Here he's referring to the number of detainees wounded, killed during the month of September while on forced labour. In reading the Coric brief, Mr. President, Your Honours, you'll see that he claims that it was, in fact, Colonel Obradovic who exercised the real authority over the HVO detention centres in Sector South, including the Heliodrom, and one of the observations I'm going to make repeatedly in my remarks is this: If indeed it was Colonel Obradovic who was in charge or responsible for these prisoners, who had the power over them, if it was Obradovic who was the one that was authorising the extensive forced labour programme that we know about, then why is it that Mr. Bozic is sending this report to Mr. Coric? And as the Trial Chamber knows and we'll discuss, Mr. Bozic sent many, many reports to Mr. Coric, and it's because he considered that it was Mr. Coric who was the person who had the authority and the capability to deal with these issues. Mr. Coric contributed to the Herceg-Bosna JCE by approving and condoning an administrative deportation system whereby prisoners gained release from HVO detention camps so long as they went home, gathered their families in Ljubuski, and left Herceg-Bosna altogether. P04263. This document, Mr. President, is dated the 17th of August, 1993. It is a document over the name of an Ante Prlic and a Jure Herceg at the 4th Brigade. Stjepan Radic, military police. He says: "Based on the order of the chief of the military police, Valentin Coric, the following detainees are to be released because they have affidavits." The document is stamped "received" by the Military Police Administration, and it gives the names of 22 individuals. Mr. President, could we briefly pass into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P04404. This is another document linked to these letters of guarantee programme. This gentleman Ante Prlic again writing: "Through this confirmation, the headquarters of the prison at Heliodrom is asked to release this prisoner, Enver Cibo, because he has an affidavit on the order of the chief of the military police." It continues: "The detainee mentioned above is to be handed over to the police Ljubuski because that is where his family is and his family has been ordered out of Herzegovina." If this was some rogue programme that no one knew about except a small group of individuals down in Ljubuski, why would this Mr. Prlic, Ante Prlic, being writing things like that the family had been ordered out of Herzegovina? And how would these people have ultimately been released if this procedure wasn't fully approved and authorised by the people who had responsibility and authority over the prisoners? Oh, and by the way, Mr. Prlic doesn't send this to Colonel Obradovic. There is no indication that Colonel Obradovic, who allegedly has the primary authority over the Heliodrom and the other prison facilities, that Colonel Obradovic was involved in this or that his approval was needed. The reference here again is consistently to Mr. Coric. P10190. This is one going not to the Heliodrom but to Gabela. So again, a communication issued from the brigade military police, this time sending the communication to Gabela, asking prisoners to be released based on an order issued by the head of the military police, Mr. Coric. They have to be delivered to the Ljubuski military police, pursuant to the fact that their families are in Ljubuski and they got expulsion from Herzegovina. These prisoners are released from the Heliodrom. They're released from Gabela. They go home, they gather their families, and they move out. P10328. The Trial Chamber may recall the evidence of Ms. Milada Orman. This is from her 92 bis statement talking about what happened in her village, Gradska, in the municipality of Ljubuski. Her testimony is consistent with what we've been seeing. Gradska is a village that makes part of Ljubuski, inhabited only by Bosniaks. They live -- there live about 1 to 200 people. When the Muslim from Ljubuski were called to report to the police station, they were called as well. When the men came back from detention, the people from Gradska organised and left on two or three buses to Zagreb. They locked their houses and left the keys in the municipality and left. They had to undergo the same procedure as other Muslim from Ljubuski. The laissez-passer, the tickets to third countries. They had a beautiful mosque in the village, and when they left, they locked it up, and they gave the key to the guardian of the church. When they went back around 1999, the mosque was completely blown up and destroyed. Some people had returned to Gradska, but not many. They want to return. The houses were not destroyed. They are occupied by Croats from middle Bosnia, but there is no power yet. So if the Trial Chamber in its deliberations wants to consider the impact of these deportation schemes on the people that lived in these areas, the Muslim population living in these areas, it has ample evidence before it in order to do that. P06135 is a report of the Spanish Battalion. I don't know that we can put it up. I can read it though. Spanish Battalion reporting on the 25th of October, 1993. "It was noticed that the mosque in the village of Gradska has been recently destroyed. Apparently the village has been vacated these days. Given that windows and doors on the houses were open and smoke was coming out of some of them, which makes one think that the population was displaced towards another places." Why was all this happening? P06232. Just four days after the Spanish Battalion made its observations on Gradska that I've just read, we have here in this exhibit, dated the 29th of October, a request coming over the name of the chief of the military police, Mr. Coric. The document itself was signed by his deputy, we believe, Mr. Lavric. Authenticity of the document has not been challenged. And here the military police is requesting the municipality to approve the following vacated apartments for temporary use by military police employees. And by now all of us are able to look at the names of the people whose apartments are being requested. We all know what the ethnicity of those individuals is. They're all Muslims. They're all gone. They've hardly left, and the military police is already looking to take over those apartments. We know that the military police had a very voracious appetite for Muslim housing, apartments, flats. P02879. This one is from the 21st of June, 1993. It's a request, again, coming from the Military Police Administration, again, Mr. Lavric signing for Mr. Coric, to the housing and infrastructure office. We request -- it's a request to issue decisions permitting occupancy of apartments: "We enclose a list of civilian apartments occupied by members of the military police. We request that the corresponding decisions be issued as urgently as possible." 137 flats, 137 members of the military police taking over these flats on the 21st of June. This is in all likelihood Mostar, West Mostar, based on the names of the streets, the locations of the flats. On this issue of the Lavric signature, we've just looked at two documents signed by him on behalf of Mr. Coric. There's been no challenge to the authenticity of the documents. It does raise the issue concerning his claims that P03220 is a forgery. It's not a forgery, just a bad document for him. The document, dated the 6th of July, 1993, when the HVO arrest campaign for all the Muslim men was getting in full swing, Colonel Obradovic absolutely expressed or sought to exert control over the release of prisoners from all four of the main camps, Heliodrom, Ljubuski, Gabela, Dretelj. He did that on a document that he issued on the preceding day. And right away, immediately, the Military Police Administration, again Lavric, signing on behalf of Coric steps right in saying that the military remand prisons are exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Military Police Administration. He tells Obradovic to cancel his order, and then he does concede that the prisoners who are in the military remand prisons and who were captured by the Knez Domagoj Brigade subordinated to Colonel Obradovic, shall be if they are released be released with your consent. Coric claims that the Lavric signature on here on his behalf is forged. It's in our brief, Mr. President. There are lots of other documents authenticity is not challenged. The signature's the same, Lavric. We see it time and time again. It's just that this particular document causes some uncomfortableness for Mr. Coric, and so he's trying to distance himself from it. I'd like to make some remarks on the issue of subordination and particularly what happened when a unit was resubordinated or sent over to fight or to be placed under the command of a different part of the HVO. Mr. Coric has made a lot of claims that once that happens, he bears no responsibility for the military police who are then subject to orders of others in the brigade and the Main Staff. It's not correct. In his testimony -- actually, in both of their testimony, General Praljak and General Petkovic told us about this issue of subordination, both of them testifying that when military police personnel were resubordinated to the brigades, they still remained military policemen. They still remained within the military police structures, and Mr. Coric continued to have responsibility for them. On the 22nd of February, 2010, at page 49795 of the transcript, General Petkovic testified: "Valentin Coric, in this specific case, would draft an order according to which a certain battalion should be subordinated in a certain area, and it will enter within the chain of command in that area. Valentin Coric, although he has subordinated the battalion to the commander, doesn't lose his responsibility over that battalion. He doesn't simply dismiss that battalion. He has the right to exercise authority over that battalion. But the commander in the area will issue them with specific tasks and will be in command of that battalion." We'll be talking a little later on about logistics and equipping the military police and how that, of course, was done, the Military Police Administration. Mr. President, if you train these individuals, if you select them, if you give them uniforms, weapons, belts, badges, and all the rest, you own them. You might lend them out to others for specific combat-related tasks, but you always own those personnel. P04186. There's a question as to who owned the prison wardens. Who were they responsible to? Mr. Coric claims that the wardens were not answerable to or were not within the chain of command or the structure of the military police. In this exhibit, 14 August 1993, Mr. Bozic, the warden at the Heliodrom facility, sends this document both to Mr. Stojic and to Mr. Coric. I'm looking at the second paragraph on the first page. Bozic says: "Because we are stationed at the barracks at the Heliodrom, we have been receiving logistics support from the 3rd Brigade the whole time due to its actual location, but the whole time we have been part of the military police unit. On a couple of occasions, leaders of the 3rd Brigade verbally warned us that they were not able to procure food for 2100 detainees, which caused us to turn to our military police unit, and they were unable to meet our request." This is consistent with testimony that came from Ljubuski. I won't give more specifics on it because it's -- it's not public. The brigade providing food, that, of course, doesn't change what units the guards, the wardens, what structures they are attached to. Mr. Bozo is here clearly telling us that he thinks he's in the military police even though it's the brigade that had been providing food for the prisoners. On the 14th of August, though, he's got a problem, because he's telling Mr. Stojic and Coric that he doesn't have food to feed these prisoners. We don't know what, if anything, Mr. Coric did about that. Mr. President, could I briefly again pass into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It makes perfect sense, of course, for things to operate -- if you're putting military police into brigades, if you're putting them into the field, they're going to have to be subject to taking orders from the units in the field, the commands in the field. Mr. Coric, throughout his brief equates the issue of exclusivity to the issue of lack of responsibility. He basically claims, "Well, the brigades could issue orders to the brigade military police, so that means I'm not responsible for them. I subordinated the 1st Light Assault Battalion to General Praljak, and so I'm not responsible for them because somebody else can give them orders. "Other people may bring people from the Heliodrom, Mr. Pusic, for example, maybe Obradovic, and since other people could exercise that authority, that means I had none. I had no responsibility." Again, this goes to the passage that my colleague Mr. Scott read from in his initial presentation, the remarks of Justice Jackson from the Nuremberg trials. You know, there are more than one -- there are multiple individuals responsible when crimes are committed. There isn't just one. And the fact that others within the Main Staff or the brigade structures could issue orders to particular members of the military police doesn't mean that Mr. Coric doesn't still bear responsibility for those members. It doesn't mean that they're no longer a part of his military police structure. The reports from the field coming in also tell us not only about the structures and the chain of command, because people don't send reports to people that are outside their chain of command. Subordinates send reports their superiors. The reports coming in also tell us a lot about knowledge and notice and the breadth of information that was available to Mr. Coric. P00648. This is the 25th of October, 1992. This is an interim report and request to take measures coming from Mr. Siljeg, commander of the north-west Herzegovina operative zone. He's sending this to the Defence Department, the Main Staff, and to the HVO Military Police Administration. He's complaining about a military police unit from Livno and Tomislavgrad that had been under the control of a Zdenko Andabak which was in Prozor and returned to Livno and Tomislavgrad with about 30 illegally seized motor vehicles. Going to the end of the document, the end of the report, Siljeg says: "I require the head of the Military Police Administration to inspect urgently military police units in Livno and Tomislavgrad. Consider the situation and take appropriate measures against individuals who behave like that." So what this tells us, Mr. President, Your Honours, is that the operative zone commander, Mr. Siljeg, he certainly believed that Mr. Coric retained authority and responsibility for the conduct of his military police subordinates, such as Mr. Andabak, out in the field, and that Mr. Coric retained the ability to take measures to deal with the misconduct. We know that in this case that at one point later Mr. Coric and General Praljak issued a joint order directing that the vehicles be returned. P05657. Excuse me, I skipped one in my outline. P02697. Mr. President, could I ask what time we're planning to take the break? I'm not sure where we are in the scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10.30 as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P02697. This is another report coming from Mr. Siljeg, this one dated now the 9th of June, 1993. He's sending this to Mr. Boban, Mr. Stojic, Petkovic, and also Mr. Coric personally. Toward the bottom of the first page, second-to-last-paragraph: "Everything is wrong in the 2nd Battalion and they cannot not be commanded, except for part of the ATG from Tomislavgrad ..." And he goes on to describe the situation: "All this indicated that the military police units in Livno, Rama, in Gornji Vakuf, are wilful, out of control, and cannot be commanded." He says: "We would request that you undertake the following measures because, you know, this is the only route for passage." And he goes on suggesting and asking for particular things to be done. In item 2: "It is true that the battalions were put under the jurisdiction of the operative zone commander, but only when we were up to our necks in problems. But what is the use of an order if there is no command and the commander is not in a position to command lower commanders or policemen, and you are conducting pursuing personnel policy in the military police." At the top of the next page, item 4, Siljeg writes: "In future, use military police from territory in the depth to secure convoys on this axis. You have been informed of all security problems regarding the flow of people and goods through Rama and other negative incidents: Murder, arson, looting ... it is high time the military police did something." Just to be completely precise, he says: "It is high time the Military Police Administration did something." The UVP. Item 6: "We are doing everything in our power ... now it is your turn." If he didn't think Mr. Coric was responsible for or could do anything about these problems he was having -- Siljeg was having with the military police in these areas, in the Prozor zone, then he wouldn't have sent this. He wouldn't have included Mr. Coric on this report. P05657. We're going to talk about the deployment of military police personnel in Mostar a bit later, but again it's worth noting here that on the 5th of October, 1993, Mr. Coric issues this order: That after having inspected the combat line in the town of Mostar, he orders that 100 military policemen are to be placed at the disposal of the Mostar town defence commander, Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic. Then he takes 20 military police from the Military Police Administration. He takes 60 military policemen out of the 5th Brigade that's based in Mostar, and another 20 policemen out of the 6th Military Police Battalion and places all of those into the Mostar town defence. So what we see here is Mr. Coric exerting direct control and his authority to deploy and to re-deploy military policemen within his own administration but outside also that administration, reaching across to his military police battalions to direct their personnel. P03090. Mr. President, this is a report on the work of the HZ-HB military police in an analysis of the situation for the period January through June 1993. It appears over Mr. Coric's name. In his brief, Mr. Coric does acknowledge that he and his Military Police Administration provided logistics support for the military police, pointing out that they issued badges and belts to the military policemen. However, he also claims, this is paragraphs 42, 128, and 217 of his brief, he claims that he received only limited reporting and that there is a multitude of evidence establishing general communications difficulties. His point being that all of these difficulties kept him out of the loop and prevented him from really knowing what was going on outside his Military Police Administration. The evidence proves otherwise. The fact is that individuals and units sent scores of reports to Coric from the field because they were part of the military police chain of command, and that command ran to Mr. Coric at the top. Here are a few of the many documents establishing that communications were operating at a highly satisfactory level and that Coric received regular reports from military police units both within the brigades and his own military police battalions. The reporting chain itself shows that all of these units, whether military police in the brigades or in the battalions remained within the sphere of responsibility of the chief of the Military Police Administration. So turning to P03090, the military police Coric report on the work for the first half of June 1993, we see on pages 26 and 27 of the English version Coric is reporting on the equipment and other items provided to his subordinates within the military police structures, camouflage trousers, jackets, et cetera, which is obviously not a surprise. And here he refers on page 27 to the 1719 white bets, white waist belts of the military police and the 499 badges. As we move down the page, however, we see that Coric won't just providing badges and belts to the military policemen. During the first half of 1993, the Military Police Administration distributed 570.000 rounds. They actually distributed more hand grenades than belts. 1719 belts versus 2506 hand grenades. They distributed 445 automatic rifles, which is roughly the same number of badges that they distributed. They distributed an even greater number of 82-millimetre mines. So the Trial Chamber has to bear that in mind when it considers Mr. Coric's claims that he wasn't responsible for what his military police people did when they were out in the field, if they were out subordinated for a combat operation to a different unit. It was Mr. Coric and his Military Police Administration that put the bullets and the guns and the hand grenades and the mines into the hands of these individuals, and he cannot absolve himself of responsibility if they use those weapons improperly and illegally. On the issue of communications, on the following pages of his report, this is page 28, he gives a very comprehensive overview of the equipment and the extent to which communications functioned throughout the Military Police Administration and, in fact, the key role that military police communications played within the HVO itself. He says that: "The state of wire communications is mainly satisfactory; all units, stations, and communication centres are connected to an automatic telephone network ..." Moving down to item 2a: "They installed repeaters in three locations for radio communications," which, he as says, "enables us to have good communications in 70 per cent of HZ-HB territory. Communications on the UHF are ensured on the level of all the battalion administrations (Ljubuski, Dretelj, Mostar, Livno, Vitez). "Radio communications cover the entire border area towards Croatia. "Generally speaking, all important check-point are well connected, and we manage to provide the optimum minimal resources for combat activities of units." Moving on, halfway down the following page Mr. Coric reports: "In addition to the said working difficulties, it is important to point out that the HVO military police communications system was the basis for ensuring communications during combat activities in the almost entire HZ-HB, and particularly in the Prozor and Mostar theatres of war, in the past period." That is January through June 1993. So communications maybe not perfect, but pretty darn good. Page 31 of this report. I'm going to step off on a different topic, but since we're on the document I think it's worth pointing this out. Section 2.4 Coric reports that: "In the past period, there were over 6.000 prisoners of war in prisons in Herceg-Bosna." Keep in mind, Mr. President, this report applies to the period of time prior to the 30 June arrest campaign that begins. Coric continues: "There are over 4.000 prisoners in the prisons. Of that number, several hundred are members of the Serbian Army, and a large number are members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, General Praljak would tell you that during this same period of time, the members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were their allies until the grand betrayal took place on the 30th of June. That is, needless to say, not the case. Coric continues: "A large number of prisoners are on work detail, which provides opportunity for escaping from prison." Never mind the problems associated with people getting shot or wounded, which as we see takes place throughout the summer of 1993. Never mind the fact that it's unlawful to use them to work in dangerous situations or to put them to work in support of the HVO war effort. The only concern here is that they might run away. They might escape. He says, moving down a few lines: "Prison wardens have been appointed, who are in charge of co-ordinating all affairs. Military police have the task of providing security for prisoners." So if the military police, their role in providing security, if the authority, the responsibilities of the wardens, didn't fall within the sphere of responsibility of the military police, why would he be writing about it in this report? Staying with P03090. This document tells us even more about the detailed level of knowledge that Mr. Coric had about the military police when they were involved in combat operations. Looking at this report, starting at pages 5, across to pages 6 and 7, he's writing about the report January through June in the north-western Herzegovina operative zone. And just turning to page 6, then, of the English, we can see the level of knowledge that he processes. He says: "When talking about this operation zone, the 2nd Light Assault Battalion should be commended for their achievements and the combat operations in Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Mostar. " ... military police took part in all major military combat operations since the beginning of the war ..." He's happy to take credit for that. Skipping down a couple paragraphs. "On 18 January 1993," we would say "at 0400," in the morning, "the overall attack was launched by the newly arrived HVO units and the HVO military police units on the villages and the dominating hill positions in the area held by the ABiH units. " ... military police units were commanded by the 1st Light Assault Battalion commander," that's Mr. Jelic, "and the 2nd Battalion commander." He goes on talking about the numbers of policemen who took over such places as the village at Uzricje, Zdrince. Continuing on to the next page: "At the same time, 2nd battalion members from Prozor took over several villages and major elevations previously controlled by ABiH ..." Down two paragraphs: On the 22nd of January ... members of the 1st Light Assault Battalion launched an attack on these villages: Rimcev Gaj, an important ABiH stronghold, the attacks started at 0400." Then he continues on. Again, if these soldiers involved in these operations weren't a part of his structure, his military police, then why would Coric be reporting about them? He's happy to take the credit. He's just not willing to take any of the blame. The fact is he equipped these soldiers. He put them in the field. He owns them, even if others in the brigade were exerting specific combat-related operational control over these soldiers in respect of these operations. P03551. What else do the reports tell us? What else do the documents tell us about Mr. Coric and his knowledge of events taking place outside of his office at the Military Police Administration? This is the 19th of July, 1993, the arrest campaign. The round-ups are in full swing throughout Herceg-Bosna and the HVO-controlled territories. This is a report of the Mostar SIS. Actually, it's Mr. Coric responding to a report of the SIS administration, the SIS officer who was up in Tomislavgrad. Coric says: "We are informing you that due to the large number of detained persons of Muslim nationality, we are unable to receive the people that, according to the aforementioned report, you are planning to send to the Mostar central military remand prison and that you should therefore keep them detained within your operations zone." This tells us that Mr. Coric had access to or read SIS reports, at least this one, if they dealt with prisoners, issues regarding prisoners, movement of prisoners. Here Mr. Coric knows how many prisoners they've got at the Heliodrom. He knows they can't take any more, and so he's having to perform some air traffic control duties, shuffling prisoners around, keeping them here, keeping them there, and exerting his power over all of them as part of a unified detention system for which he bears a key, key role. P05497. In terms of reporting and in terms of Mr. Coric's knowledge and the structures, the structures of the military police that provided him with knowledge, let's spend a couple of minutes talking about his 5th Military Police Battalion based in Mostar. It had companies throughout the south-east Herzegovina operative zone. Up until June it's the 3rd Military Police Battalion, until he did the reorganisation. This exhibit, Mr. President, is a monthly report on the work of the 5th Military Police Battalion for the month of September 1993. On page 2, what we see here -- actually, on the bottom of page 1 they say: "Security. During the past month, the 5th Military Police Battalion guarded facilities and persons of special importance as follows." And then on page 2 we get a very extensive list of all the places where members of Mr. Coric's 5th military police battalion are out providing security. They are providing security to people who are linked to the HZ-HB government, such as Mr. Boban himself in Grude. That's towards the bottom of the page. But of course, more significantly, we see them providing security, that is, guards for the HVO prison camps. About the sixth line down from the top of this page: "Security of the central military detention facility at the Heliport - 21 military policemen." Moving down a few lines: Security at the Dretelj barracks - 6 military policemen. Security of prisoners at Dretelj - 10 military policemen. Security at the military police station in Stolac, Neum, security at the military police centre Ljubuski, health centre, Citluk. He's got subordinates in his 5th Military Police Battalion throughout the south-east Herzegovina operative zone, all of whom are sending him reports, all of whom are giving him information about events in the field, many of whom are directly guarding the prisoners in the prison facilities. Down toward the bottom they've got 23 military policemen at the military detention facility in Ljubuski. The bottom of the page summing up: "Hence in September, 174 members of the 5th Military Police Battalion worked on security jobs." The bottom of page 4, continuing on page 5 of this report: "Traffic check-points. The 5th Military Police Battalion manned 19 permanent traffic check-points, namely ..." all these places you see on the following page. Moving ahead to paragraph 14. What else is in this report? Third page -- third paragraph toward the bottom: "Checking the security of the prisoners at the Heliport, we found out that prisoners being taken to work at the front line did not all return and that a large number are wounded and mutilated." In another report, this time coming from within his own 5th Military Police Battalion to Coric on what's happening with the prisoners out at the Heliodrom facility. Bottom of page 16. This goes to the Military Police Administration. This report also goes to Mr. Coric. The Trial Chamber might find the table that's attached to this report at page 17 of the English to be of use when it considers what units fell within this 5th Military Police Battalion that's reporting to Mr. Coric. It's all laid out here in this table. We see the battalion command. We see the companies. The companies themselves are based out in the field in places like Capljina, Ljubuski, elsewhere. And then we see references to the brigade platoons; that is, the brigade military police who are within -- who are themselves situated within a brigade but who, nonetheless, remain within the structure of the 5th Military Police Battalion. Jumping back to P039 -- sorry, P03090, the report of Mr. Coric on the work of the military police for January through June 1993. This is an organigramme chart that's attached to the report. It tells us what units are sitting directly under him, and what we see again is an assistant chief for the south-east Herzegovina operative zone. Underneath Mr. Coric, underneath Mr. Lavric who was the deputy chief of the Military Police Administration. Then we see in the Mostar area, south-east Herzegovina, we see a light assault battalion, and we see a 5th Battalion, and then we see the same structure in other places. So again there's no question. We can -- we can parse words about what happened when the 1st Light Assault Battalion was subordinated to General Praljak and the Main Staff on the 29th of August, 1993, but there are military police personnel out there who are not touched by the issue of subordination, and those are the members of the 5th Military Police Battalion, and those are the brigade military police. But all of them, including the members of the 1st Light Assault Battalion, when the subordination takes place in late August of 1993, all of them remain military police, all remain under the control of Mr. Coric. He's the one who has the power over them. Mr. President, this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court's back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'm going to stay with the issue of reporting within the military police structure. However, could I ask that we very briefly again pass into private session for one short remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P03401 is a report dated 12 July 1993 from the 4th Brigade Military Police at Ljubuski. In terms of what's being reported to the police, Military Police Administration, Mr. President, I wanted to note here at the bottom of page 1: "In Rama the military police arrested 237 Muslims and took them to the Ljubuski prison. Commander Prlic contacted Capljina military police commander Ancic and military police chief Valentin Coric and obtained approval to transfer the above prisoners to the Dretelj military prison in Capljina. A patrol of the brigade military police took them to Capljina." The report continues: "On Mr. Tomic's orders we took 20 prisons," it says, "with a military police escort to IZM," that's the forward command post, "for labour. They were returned to the prison in the evening ..." If we move forward to the next exhibit which is P03121. We see now a report coming out of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Military Police Battalion in Capljina. Now, Mr. President, again this is not brigade military police. This is the 3rd Company of the 3rd Military Police Battalion. This is in July. This would be on the 2nd of July, 1993. This is a report of the commander of the 3rd Company there, Mr. Kresimir Bogdanovic reporting. And again, going to the end of the document just quickly to see that this has been delivered to the command of the 3rd Battalion and also to the Military Police Administration. This is reporting that ten military policemen guarded the Dretelj barracks where the arrested Muslims are held. There were no problems. He goes on the next day saying that: "One Military Police Platoon in Stolac was used for collecting Muslims ..." He makes reference farther down on the page to check-points and the role that the check-points played and how useful the check-points were as part of the campaign that was underway. Again, this is being the 2nd of July, 1993. The "... check-points used, especially to those leading towards Muslim-inhabited places, because it can be expected that many Muslims will try to hide, which would make the arrest very difficult." He continues: "The task of bringing in was carried out by Knez Domagoj, 1st Brigade, brigade police, members of the Capljina MUP, and our members who brought in persons addressed at check-point." Going on to the next page, he reports: "In the afternoon, six buses with Muslims were brought in from the Heliodrom. All persons brought in were accommodated in buildings of the Dretelj barracks and a proper record of them is kept." P03055 is related to this last point. This is dated the previous day, the 1st of July, 1993. This is an order -- actually, it's a document made by Mr. Zvonko Vidovic and Mr. Stanko Bozic reporting the order by Berislav Pusic to transfer 200 detainees from the central military police prison in Mostar to the prison in Capljina until further notice. So again, what we see here is the order from Pusic sending 200 prisoners down to the prison in Capljina, and the previous document, P03121, we have Mr. Coric's subordinate in the 3rd Military Police Battalion, Mr. Bogdanovic, reporting that in fact the Muslims arrived on the buses from the Heliodrom. So this tells us a couple of things. It tells us first of all that this is all taking place within one uniform, unified prison system, falling within the competence and authority of the military police in which the prisoners were held and moved and transferred in ways that suited the captors, Mr. Coric, Mr. Pusic, and the others. Again, no reference to Colonel Obradovic here as having any role to play in the approval on the transfer of these prisoners even though, according to the Coric Defence, Mr. Obradovic was the one who possessed exclusive and overall authority concerning all the detention facilities located in the operative zone of south-east Herzegovina, including the prison of Heliodrom. That's what Mr. Coric says in paragraphs 460 and 468 of his brief. I'm going to pass over the next exhibit, which was P03347. It's another exhibit from Mr. Bogdanovic. I'm trying to stay on my time since we got off to a little bit of a late start today. I'd like to move on to P05869, staying again with the issue of reporting and what units within the military police structure were reporting to Mr. Coric and what types of information was he getting from them. This is a 14 October 1993 report of the -- the minutes, actually, of the regular monthly meeting of leading officers of the Military Police Administration and military police battalion commanders. The meeting was held on the 10th of October. Mr. Coric is named first among these present, followed by Mr. Lavric, the assistant chief, and others whose names appear on page 2 of the document. The point here is not what the minutes say themselves but what's on the agenda. What does this tell us about what was on the agenda at this meeting? "Item 1. Submission of reports on work during the preceding month." Then moving down: "Item 1. Reporting --" it says: "Reports on work during the preceding month were submitted and comprehensively discussed and analysed by those present." "Item 2. On the basis of the reports submitted on work and the current situation and the priority tasks of the military police having been assessed, the meeting issued the following." They issue their conclusions. The point being there are regular monthly meetings that Mr. Coric had with all of his commanders, subordinate commanders, and in those meetings, all of the month's reports are comprehensively discussed. In regard -- I want to focus a bit on the situation involving forced labour and the use of prisoners from the Heliodrom for that. It's confidential, so we're not going to put it up, but the Trial Chamber may have looked at confidential Annex M to the Prosecution's final trial brief in this case. It contains a table with some 100 -- excuse me, 235 orders issued approving the use of prisoners for forced labour, the vast majority of those orders on forced labour having been issued by a Zlatan Mijo Jelic, Mr. Coric's direct subordinate, and commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion. The primary overwhelming beneficiary of the forced labour of the prisoners from the Heliodrom being the 1st Light Assault Battalion itself. There is no indication on any of these approvals for the release of prisoners for forced labour that Colonel Obradovic played any role in this process. P04259 is a report dated 17 August, 1993. It is one of many reports made by Stanko Bozic, the warden at the Heliodrom facility. His many reports directly to Mr. Coric, informing Coric about the prisoners who were being killed and wounded in Mostar while performing forced labour. Mr. Bozic's reports to Mr. Coric on that are contained as well in the Prosecution's confidential Annex M. In this Exhibit P04259, we see Bozic reporting that the prisoners, 90 inmates, had been turned over for labour on the 13th of August, and then they received a report that ten of them had been wounded. This report went to Mr. Coric and also Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic. Mr. Bozic would not be sending this report and all the others to Mr. Coric if he didn't consider Mr. Coric to be the one with responsibility for the prisoners being held at the Heliodrom facility. Mr. President, could we please go into private session for one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a few documents on the issue of separation of prisoners detained, in this case in the Heliodrom. The Defence have argued, General Praljak has argued, I know General Petkovic has argued or testified that only Muslim members who had been members of the HVO were used for forced labour. P04675. This is a report of Mr. Bozic dated 31 August 1993. He's noting or reporting that 60 detainees were handed over for work. One was killed, Asim Drljevic, and that on that occasion nine detainees were wounded. Only four were kept in the hospital for treatment, and the four are named. The first one of those being Mr. Almir Spuzevic. P04680. This is a report coming from a different source on the same day, 31 August 1993, informing today two prisoners were killed, 25 wounded while they were working in Ricina Street. And then the wounded are identified. There are 26 names appearing there. And on the second page, number 16, is a Sanel Muslic, born in 1975. This document bears the stamp of the -- the "Received" stamp of the Military Police Administration. So focusing on those two, Mr. Spuzevic and Mr. Muslic, what was their status? Were they former members, Muslim members of the HVO? No, they're not. P03013 is a list of persons detained in the military remand prison centre on the 30th of June, 1993, the day the arrest campaign began. There are many, many persons indicated or listed on this list, and there are many lists like this for the same day and the days that followed. On page 23 of the English version of the list -- excuse me, page 4 of the English version, item number 23, there is a reference here to Almir Spuzevic who we just saw was wounded on the 31st of August, 1993, as noted in the report of Bozic. The list from the 30th of June tells us that he was residing in Mostar and that he was not engaged at the -- in the military at the time he was arrested on the 30th of June. So this tells us that during the entire month of July and the entire month of August until the end on the 31st, when he was wounded working on the front line, Mr. Spuzevic remained in the HVO custody, and throughout this entire period of time the HVO's own records tells us that he had not been engaged in the military. He was a civilian. Page 7 of the same list of prisoners, item 56, refers to a Samir, son of Ibrahim Muslic, born on 11 February 1975 in Mostar. 11 February 1975, make him 18 years old. So he is military age. He's still quite a young man. He, in our submission, is the other individual who's listed on the report from 31 August as having been wounded while working on the front line. So this tells us that he also had been in the Heliodrom for a full two months and that their records, their own records tell us that he was not engaged in the military. He was not a former HVO member. If you look at this page and throughout this document P03013, the Trial Chamber will see many, many references to individuals who were not in the military. A couple of them on this page even deemed unfit for military service. That's the person at number 48, or the gentleman number 54, who was not engaged in the military. He had a heart attack. These are civilians, and we know that the civilians were held, detained, together with POWs, together with Muslims who had been members of the HVO. There was no separation as required under international humanitarian law, and the Trial Chamber has our submissions on that issue in our final trial brief. In his -- in his final trial brief, Mr. Coric, rather remarkably, in the Prosecution's submission, points the finger for the forced labour responsibility to none other than the prison wardens such as Mr. Bozic himself, who sent scores of reports directly to Mr. Coric, to Mr. Jelic, and others complaining about the use of the forced labourers, reporting diligently the numbers wounded, the numbers killed. Paragraph 475 of the Coric brief says: "Documentary evidence proved the responsibility of the prison wardens with regard to labour of prisoners." And they cite some documents on that, including P04233. In fact, what does 4233 say? This is dated 16 August 1993. It's a letter to the -- Mr. Zarko Tole who was the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. It's sent by a member of Mr. Coric's 5th Military Police Battalion, Mr. Josip Praljak, who as the Trial Chamber will recall was the deputy warden of the Heliodrom facility, working with Mr. Bozo. And in this document, this communication to the Main Staff, Mr. Josip Praljak says -- he refers to: "... photocopies of reports which were submitted on time in order to put a stop to the practice of the military police who take detainees away for labour. "Sir, we request you as chief to forbid such behaviour by the soldiers who take them away for labour, and also that delinquent behaviour be most severely punished." So rather than implicating the prison wardens in the crime of forced labour, which is what Mr. Coric attempts to do with this document, the document, in fact, shows that the prison warden, in this case the deputy, Mr. Praljak, was reaching out to the Main Staff because they were not getting any support. They weren't getting any reaction whatsoever from Mr. Coric as the chief of the Military Police Administration in their attempts to bring this widespread practice of forced labour, the many woundings, and the many deaths that were taking place to Mr. Coric's attention. It's not the only desperate attempt to try to get someone to do something about this. We will see later that Mr. Stanko Bozic did the same thing, directing his concerns directly to the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban. Mr. President, I would like to take a few minutes to return to the issue of resubordination now that we've been talking about forced labour and the role of the commander of the military police's 1st Light Assault Battalion in approving forced labour, that is Mr. Jelic, and the fact that the military police 1st Light Assault Battalion was a primary beneficiary and participant in the use of forced labourers in Mostar. Mr. Coric asked the Trial Chamber to consider the fact that in late August, on the 28th of August, 1993, he subordinated the military police 1st Light Assault Battalion to Mr. Praljak and the HVO Main Staff. That is P03763. There's no dispute about this. General Praljak testified about it. He asked for it. He got it. Mr. Coric by this order is putting the 1st light assault battalions, including the 1st Light Assault Battalion commanded by Mijo Jelic, resubordinating them operationally for purposes of combat operations to the commander of the HVO Main Staff. Mr. Coric's argument here is that because he did this, because the Main Staff took away members of the 1st Light Assault Battalion and other Light Assault Battalion personnel as well, this prevented him from fighting crime and using these soldiers to fight crime and to do real policemen work, military police work, in Mostar. So if the Trial Chamber is going to consider that argument that Mr. Coric's intentions were all good and benign and that he would have done more about crime if he'd just had the military police personnel, General Praljak hadn't taken them away, it's worth considering what the military police policing activity was, and particularly the activities of the 1st Light Assault Battalion in Mostar were before the resubordination took place late in July 1993. P02802. This is a report of the 3rd battalion of the military police in Mostar, dated the 15th of June, 1993. So this is before there's any subordination. Stamped "Received" at the Military Police Administration. Mr. President, Your Honours, you'll note first of all that the report indicates, page 1, that yesterday, the 1st Company wrote an eviction order for the apartment located here as indicated on the document, again indicating the military police continued participation in the taking of flats in Mostar. Passing over to the next page. Mate Ancic, who wrote this, states that: "No criminal acts or incidents were notified yesterday. Only the ethnical cleansing of the town from Muslims -- persons of Muslim nationality was noticed." He says: "The perpetrators were members of the 4th Battalion and members of the ATG ..." So that gives the Trial Chamber some idea of how strongly the military police in Mostar were combatting crime before any issues of resubordination came up in late July of 1993. We can look very briefly again at P02879 from roughly the same period of time. This is the document we saw earlier. This is the request from Mr. Lavric on behalf of Mr. Coric at the Military Police Administration, asking that the occupancy be permitted of all of these apartments for 137 members of the military police in Mostar. We know, of course, this is happening right in the midst of a violent campaign of expulsions in West Mostar that kicked off particularly after the events of the 9th and 10th of May, 1993. So we know what the military police was doing about apartments before any resubordination took place. They were taking apartments of people who were being evicted from their homes. Now, I'm going to come back to confidential Annex M. We're not going to put it up because it's confidential. If the Trial Chamber looks at the table, the Trial Chamber is going to see some 36 orders approving the use of forced labourers by Mr. Jelic, commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion prior to the 28th of July when this Light Assault Battalion was subordinated to General Praljak. So that tells us that the Light Assault Battalion and Mr. Jelic were highly engaged in the practice of the use of illegal forced labourers from the Heliodrom before any subordination took place. And if you go back to confidential Annex M, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber will see, of course, that Mr. Jelic and the 1st Light Assault Battalion continued to used prisoners at a huge rate after they were subordinated by Mr. Coric to the Main Staff on the 28th, 29th of August, 1993. So in this respect, subordination plays no role. It has no impact whatsoever in respect of these crimes. We know that it was Mr. Jelic approving the use of all of these forced labourers as indicated in all of these many orders, and having done so on the authority of Valentin Coric. This is P00352. It's page 27. This is from the diary of deputy warden Josip Praljak who we just saw writing the Main Staff asking them to do something about forced labour. We know he reports that on the 4th of July they were asking Bozic whether to taken prisoners for work. Bozic says: "I approve for the barracks and the military police for the outside, but I will ask the chief." The next Josip Praljak reports meeting with Bozic where Bozic informs: "As of today, nobody can take prisoners to perform labour without written approval signed by Mijo Jelic and his deputy Dedo Primorac." Mr. President, the evidence establishes that it was Mr. Coric who Mr. Bozic himself tells us through his many, many reports to Coric that it was Coric who processed the authority and who then delegated the authority to approve prisoner release for purposes of forced labour. He delegated that to Mr. Jelic, his subordinate and commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion, and also to Mr. Primorac. And consistent with that in confidential Annex M, the Trial Chamber will see the many, many scores of orders for approving forced labour that were issued by those two individuals. It bears noting that Coric concedes in paragraph 484 of his brief that Mr. Jelic remained a member of the military police even after he was appointed to the Mostar defence. Mr. Jelic was at all times a military police officer, and he was at all times a direct subordinate of Mr. Coric. Mr. President, can we pass into private session for what I think will be the last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P05554. Again, getting back to this question of the impact on military policing duties of the redeployment of the military police 1st Light Assault Battalion to General Praljak at the end of August 1993, here we see a report dated the 1st of October. It's not a military police report. It's a report of the SIS. It reports the abduction of Muslims from Centar to suburb in Mostar on the 29th of September, reporting that Vinko Martinovic, Stela, convicted in this Trial Chamber of these very crimes, arrived at the Mostar defence, which at the time was under the command of Mr. Jelic. When he did not find him, he went to find the deputy commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion, Mr. Cavar, who obviously knew about the operation because he had already prepared a blueprint of the operation, apartment stickers "Under military police control" printed on them, and how many people would take part in the operation. Again we see the military police's appetite for Muslim housing in West Mostar even at this period, late September 1993. The transfer was drawn up, the transfer of women and children to the left bank, men to the Heliodrom to be kept for labour, of course. The plan also envisaged seizing all apartment keys and placing stickers on apartment doors. Moving across to the next page. The last statement: "The commander of the Mostar Defence sector, Zlatan Jelic, aka Mijo, was also informed of this operation subsequently, and Colonel Ivan Andabak ..." Now, what this tells us, Mr. President, is the fact that Mr. Coric had deployed, resubordinated, the 1st Light Assault Battalion to Mr. Praljak one month earlier had no impact whatsoever on policing duties in Mostar. The 1st Light Assault Battalion was itself engaged in a high level of crime in Mostar during this very period of time. It didn't matter whether they were directly subordinated to General Praljak or whether they say -- remained strictly under the structure of the Military Police Administration, they were a part of the problem and nothing they did was going to help with dealing with the core crimes that were taking place in Mostar. And I'm talking about the big picture, the big-ticket items, the appropriation of Muslim property, for example, Muslim housing; the deportations of Muslims from West Mostar across the river. These are core crimes linked directly to the achievement of the Herceg-Bosna plan, and there's no evidence that the military police has ever policed those crimes. I'm going to pass now to a bit of the Trial Chamber judgement in the Milutinovic, which contains some very relevant language that we submit is useful to the Trial Chamber in analysing this question of punishment. This is what they said in the Milutinovic case: "Documents from the Pristina Corps command and subordinate units demonstrate that some measures were undertaken at different levels against members of the Pristina Corps units who were found to have committed crimes of murder, rape ... robbery. Although it has been concluded above that the few prosecutions of VJ members in Kosovo were manifestly inadequate in light of the scale of offences occurring there, the Chamber finds that this evidence shows that Lazarevic undertook some punitive measures against subordinates responsible for the crimes of murder and rape, along with property crimes. However, the Chamber notes that the evidence does not demonstrate any prosecutions undertaken or punishments imposed in respect of the forcible expulsion of Kosovo Albanians by VJ members. It considers that the widespread commission of forcible displacement, as detailed in Section VII and the lack of criminal prosecutions for such acts does support the Prosecution contention that Lazarevic intentionally failed to ensure prosecutions of subordinates responsible for forcibly displacing Kosovo Albanians." Now, Mr. President, the Prosecution will be the first to tell you and to agree that within the Military Police Administration, within the companies, within the 5th Military Police Battalion, there were good men, and they were trying to do a good job. They were trying to do something about the widespread crime that was happening there. That's why they're writing all these reports that we've been looking at. And there's no question that individuals were punished and prosecuted for some robberies or rapes or murders. Mr. Coric, as he points out in his brief, he -- he issued disciplinary measures against four members of the military police who had been members of Dr. Prlic's security detail. They -- they'd committed rape. They were kicked out of the military police. So it may be that people, maybe the accused, maybe Mr. Coric didn't want people to be raped, and maybe he didn't want people to be murder, but the evidence shows that he, like the other accused, wanted them gone, and we don't see any evidence of any law enforcement energy being put into dealing with the big-ticket crimes, the crimes as indicated in -- in the Milutinovic judgement, the crimes linked to the forcible displacement, the taking of the flats, the crimes that really lead to the large numbers of people being thrown out. There's no evidence of that in this case even if there is some evidence of a prosecution or a disciplinary measure here and there being meted for a rape or a murder. We see this in P03616, which are the minutes of a meeting, a meeting held of a working group on crime in Mostar. Working group on combatting and detecting perpetrators. And on page 2 we see Mr. Mladen Jurisic, who is the military prosecutor speaking. And again, this is in -- on the 21st of July, 1993, right as the expulsions are in full swing. I think it's the same day as -- as -- I could be wrong. At the same period of time when Muslims are being expelled in droves across the Neretva River, Mr. Jurisic says: "We are now overloaded with charges of failure to respond to mobilisation orders, overloaded with charges against war criminals, and also charges against members of the Muslim armed forces, but there are no charges against criminals in the town of Mostar." It's as indicated in the report we saw a few moments ago, all is quiet. No crime reported. We're just noting the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from West Mostar, because in the culture of the military police, that was not criminal conduct. That's a core crime linked to the achievement of the Herceg-Bosna JCE, and it was not dealt with at all by the Military Police Administration. Mr. President, we know -- and I think this may be a confidential document, so we won't put it up. P11220 tells us that in March of 1995 Mr. Coric as the minister of the interior of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna appointed Mijo Jelic to be the head of the Special Police sector of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So this elite unit, as how it's reported in this article, is one that's to be headed by an individual appointed by Coric to manage the authorisations for hundreds of prisoners to be taken to work on forced -- on the confrontation lines for forced labour, who allowed members of his 1st Light Assault Battalion to take part in ethnic cleansing operations directly in West Mostar. So this tells us volumes about Mr. Coric's views about the utility that Mr. Jelic played in achieving the goals of the Herceg-Bosna JCE. The last exhibit is P05792. Mr. President, we've been talking about the many reports sent to Mr. Coric from the field, Capljina, Dretelj, Heliodrom. Mr. Siljeg at the operative zone sending reports down to Mostar, trying to get Mr. Coric to do something about the criminal conduct of the military police in the north-west Herzegovina operative zone. Those aren't the only people that thought Mr. Coric had the authority to make things right. I spoke earlier about Josip Praljak, who out of desperation finally wrote directly to the Chief of Staff of the HVO Main Staff, Mr. Tole, complaining to them about the use of prisoners for forced labour, the woundings and the killings that were resulting from it. Here in this we see -- this is a long letter written by Mr. Bozic directly to the President of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Boban. On page 2, item number 1, he's requesting a solution to these problems so as to ease the work of the prison. And he points out taking detained persons away for work. Item number 2, "Serious injuries and suffering of detainees." And he goes on. What we see in the written notation at the top of the document is that President Boban read this and wrote to the chief of the military police, Valentin Coric: "This is a very serious problem. Please contact Mr. Bozic. Sort the matter out within the limits of what is possible and the requirements of humanitarian law." This is the 10th of October, 1993. We know that prisoners continued to be taken for forced labour after this. We know what the conditions were like throughout the remainder of 1993. We know that most importantly, perhaps for our purposes, the president of Herceg-Bosna himself thought Mr. Coric was the one who had the responsibility, the authority, and the capability to deal with these problems. We, of course, know otherwise, because we've seen the many notices and the reports that were sent to Mr. Coric. He knew very well all the crimes that were taking place. He did nothing about forced labour. The military police continued to take part in ethnic cleansing operations in West Mostar and continued to move their own personnel into the flats and homes that were left behind after the Muslims moved out. Mr. President, later we'll have some final submissions about Mr. Coric. That completes my remarks for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I believe it is now Mr. Kruger who will take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon everybody in and around the courtroom. Your Honours, I will be presenting the concluding remarks for Mr. Berislav Pusic, accused number six. It's regrettable that he's not in the courtroom today, but we trust that he will be watching these proceedings on the monitor. Your Honours, the essence of Mr. Pusic's defence is summed up in the very first paragraph of his final trial brief, and if we can just call that up on the monitor. Your Honour, it seems we've already run into a problem. I don't have that slide on the monitor, but I can read it for the Trial Chamber. The very first paragraph says: "Pusic was a low-ranking civil servant involved in a technical and administrative capacity in the exchange and release of prisoners with no de jure or de facto powers to give orders to anyone else or to interfere in the operation of Croatian Defence council detention centres. Pusic principally rubber stamped decisions taken by the other HVO bodies and officials. Pusic was a small and disposable cog in the bureaucratic wheel, not an independent decision-maker who could exert control over the policies and practices of the HVO." Your Honours, if this assertion is accepted, and the Prosecution does not accept his version, if this is accepted, Mr. Pusic has immediately, in the very first paragraph of his summary of his own role and position in the HVO, exposed himself to conviction and a sentence of imprisonment in accordance with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Kvocka case precisely provided how view the role of a low-ranking disposable administrative cog in a JCE. And I would like to refer to the accused Prcac in particular in the Prosecutor versus Kvocka et al. He worked for 22 days in the Omarska camp where he used to handle lists of detainees, deal with particulars of newly arrived detainees, take care of the transfer of detainees from one camp to another, and manage the movement of detainees within the camp. If we can look specifically at paragraphs 448 and 449. According to the Trial Chamber, Prcac was fully aware of the ongoing system of abuse pervading the camp. Paragraph 457 says despite this, he continued to work for 22 days in the Omarska camp where he performed his duties efficiently, effectively, and indifferently, and with deliberate care and diligence. Now, Your Honours, if we move down to paragraph 459, the Trial Chamber said: "Prcac was the administrative aid to the commander of the camp," and we see that he was "carrying lists detainees ..." And then if we could turn to paragraph 460 of that judgement. At the end it says: "The role Prcac played in the functioning of the camp provided a valuable service and his administrative duties constituted one of the many integral cogs in the wheel of a system of gross mistreatment."
