The Trial Chamber found though Prcac did not participate directly in the commission of any crimes, he was guilty of co-perpetrating the crimes of persecution, murder, and torture as part of the JCE, and they sentenced him to about five years' imprisonment, and on appeal this was confirmed, his conviction. With respect, if the Pusic defence is accepted, these same paragraphs pretty much describe the role of Mr. Pusic, he should then properly be convicted as at least a co-perpetrator of the crimes committed as part of the JCE. Your Honours, the Prosecution, however, asserts that Pusic was much more than only a slowly level administrative technician, disposable cog that he portrays himself to be. His liability lies at a much higher level. Before stepping off the Kvocka judgement, it should be noted that regarding accused Prcac, the JCE in Omarska camp was formed on 27 May 1993. Mr. Prcac only joined that JCE weeks later, starting work there on 15 July 1993. Neither the Trial Chamber nor the Appeals Chamber had any problem in convicting Mr. Prcac as a member of that JCE. Mr. Pusic's argument, that indictment paragraph 230, the so-called exclusion clause, is incompatible with having Pusic as a leading member of the JCE has no basis in law. And that's in his brief from paragraph -- page 20 onwards. The Tribunal law recognises that a person can join a JCE at a later stage. And, of course, it's only fair then to hold such a person responsible only for the crimes committed from the time of joining onwards. Now, Your Honours, back to Mr. Pusic's first paragraph of his trial brief. He asserts his defence is based on a careful analysis of the evidence. The "careful analysis" he refers to consists of highlighting very selectively and in isolation certain snippets of evidence and testimony and arguing on the basis thereof that all the Prosecution evidence, which points to Pusic's membership and participation in the JCE, actually doesn't prove this at all. On paper he says, "I had power, but in reality, I had none." Pusic, in putting this forward as a serious defence, however, is confronted with several dilemmas in order to make it work. The first dilemma for the Pusic defence, Your Honours, is that -- that the Pusic Defence has already presented all of their current arguments to the Chamber previously during their 98 bis submissions in January 2008. In its 98 bis decision, the Trial Chamber found as follows after considering all the evidence, and this is at transcript page 27236 to 237, on 20 February 2008: "In light of the above evidence, a reasonable Trial Chamber could find beyond any reasonable doubt that the Accused Pusic held a leadership position and shared the common criminal purpose of deporting Muslims from the territory of Herceg-Bosna by force and other criminal means, and that he participated in the joint criminal enterprise through his acts and omissions as an officer of the HVO military police in charge of the exchanges of Bosnian Muslims detained by the HVO, as the chief of the service in charge of the exchange of prisoners and other persons, and as the president in charge of the commission in charge of all the Herceg-Bosna prisons and detention facilities." Since that time, Your Honours, the Pusic Defence has not placed any alternative evidence before this court. No evidence whatsoever which could convincingly persuade the Trial Chamber to come to a different conclusion. The dilemma for the Pusic Defence is that the Trial Chamber must therefore assess Pusic's criminal liability for the crimes he is charged with on the basis of the very same evidence they have already previously found sufficient beyond any reasonable doubt. The second dilemma for the Pusic Defence is that Pusic actually concedes that the evidence before the Trial Chamber shows him possessing and exerting authority. To surmount this dilemma, Pusic simply asserts that the Court should place absolutely no store by all of this because he didn't any power. Therefore, when he says, "I acknowledge what I said in 1993 and what all of the evidence points to, but ignore this and accept when I tell you that I actually had no power or authority." And that brings us to the third dilemma. The -- Pusic's claim that he had no power and authority is not based on any evidence, because he's put none before the Court. It is based only on the bare assertions of Pusic in his final trial brief. The irony is that Pusic asserts that he exaggerated or lied about his authority in 1993, and this is in his final trial brief at page 39. However, now, when he is faced with the possibility of imprisonment, Pusic says he's speaking the truth when he says he didn't have any authority. Now, this is the dilemma for the Pusic Defence. They have to acknowledge that Mr. Pusic was -- has a track record of being a liar and an opportunist, while at the same time trying to convince the Trial Chamber that what he is asserting now is the truth and not an opportunistic attempt to stay out of prison. The Prosecution respectfully submits that Mr. Pusic's simple assertions of his innocence, unsupported by any sworn testimony or alternative evidence from him, is not sufficient to overcome these dilemmas. Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that it has convincingly set out in its 98 bis arguments on 5 February 2008, and now again in its Prosecution final trial brief in even more detail, how the evidence before the Chamber concerning Berislav Pusic proves beyond a reasonable doubt that his membership and participation in the JCE charged and how he is variously criminally liable for the crimes he's charged with. All the evidence for each allegation against Berislav Pusic is specifically, comprehensively, and clearly cited, and the evidence is not incidental, anecdotal, or imaginary. It is convincing and consistent, showing Pusic's role in the JCE spanning several months, from April 1993 onwards. All this evidence points to his large-scale involvement and participation in the JCE, and on this the Prosecution and the Pusic Defence are essentially in agreement. However, the Pusic Defence asserts that the Prosecution is wrong to accept that all this evidence is proof of Mr. Pusic's significant participation. No, once again they say, ignore this evidence. Although it seems to point his large-scale involvement, it simply isn't true, because Pusic tended to exaggerate his own power and authority; Pusic final trial brief, paragraphs 120 to 123. Witnesses and the Prosecution exaggerate or overstate his power and authority; that's the Pusic final trial brief, paragraphs 87, 128, 176, 217 and 248. And then all the documents, orders, and approvals bearing his signature have no value. He was merely a rubber stamp for others who exerted the true authority. Now, in Berislav Pusic -- in his view, he was little more than a secretary in 1993 and 1994, rather than what the evidence shows - a ruthless corrupt military policeman who guised ethnic cleansing in the systematic detention and exchange of Muslim men, women, and children. Your Honours, to find for Mr. Pusic on the basis of his arguments, the Trial Chamber must accept Mr. Pusic's interpretation of the evidence. The problem for Mr. Pusic is his silent and passive defence. He did not provide the Trial Chamber with any evidence to support his interpretation. The Trial Chamber has only his unsworn and untested word in the form of his final trial brief, and perhaps his earlier 98 bis submissions. It's worth taking a moment to consider what evidence there is to throw some light on Mr. Pusic the man. Despite not having testified, there's ample evidence that sheds light on his character and integrity. And I'd like to turn first to Exhibit P00663. This is an official notice by the HVO SIS on October 28, 1993. And it records, paragraph 1 on page 1: "On the occasion of the search of the house owned by Berislav Pusic, a member of the military police ...," and then it mentions which authorities were searching, did the search, "... who had noticed that the Pusic brothers, Berislav and Vitomir, were regularly delivering stolen goods to the house. Each week, one or two stolen vehicles, or the vehicles confiscated from the Serbs using forged certificates ... that were issued by Berislav ..." Continuing on the same page, paragraph 2: "Berislav Pusic together with his brother Vito and Makso opened a shop in Rudnik and were procuring goods by stealing the international aid and the Caritas aid." And page 2 still, on page 2: "During the war," and this is 1992, the war with the Serbs, "Berislav Pusic was issuing certificates to the Serbs ..." And then at the bottom: Berislav Pusic -- or "Pusic was destroying documents in the Mostar county prison at the request of some Serbs, and he was probably receiving certain amounts of (foreign currency) for doing the favour." Paragraph 3: " ... he," Pusic, "was protecting the Serbs ... releasing them from the Mostar county prison and destroying documents. And then: "In addition this, they were making a list of persons of Serb nationality for the exchange and, according to some information, they were requesting money for it, so those persons who did not have the money would leave the keys of their flats to Pusic, who would then take all the valuable property out of the flat." This was 1992. Now, Your Honours a year later, in December 1993, the SIS produced a further report, and this is Exhibit P07007 of the 2nd of December 1993, and on the second page we see that the report is regarding the work and behaviour of Berislav Pusic. Page 2, it says: "Berislav Pusic worked in the SDB in the former Communist state. For a small material gain, Pusic sold information to criminals against whom an operation was being prepared ... the operation failed ... and Pusic was fired." Continues: "After the work broke out in Mostar, Pusic, using the fact that he had been fired from the UDBA, to be engaged -- he used that fact to be engaged in the military police of the HVO." Further on the same page: "Pusic immediately got down to work. Mrs. Cesic, who used to be a typist in the military police, would type a certificate." And then the procedure is described, and it says: "Pusic signed the certificates, stamped them, and sold them to these people for 200 Deutschmarks a piece." And page 3 at the top: "During the war against the Chetniks, Pusic arrested the famous photographer Braco Njunjic." And then we see that he extorted the following from him: 5.000 Deutschmarks; six slot machines, valued at 30.000 Deutschmarks; a cannon photocopying machine, valued at 2.500 Deutschmarks; and a Peugeot 205 ..." Also on page -- just after that we see that he took 8.000 Deutschmarks from Miso Grcic, but despite that he kept him in custody for months. "Pusic sent Grcic to be exchanged on three occasions against his will." Still page 3: "... it was discovered that Pusic took money on a daily basis from people who were free and from those who were in detention for various favours ..." On page 4: "Soldiers had a joke call him Berko Pusic also known as '200 Deutschmarks.'" Now, Your Honours, this was all in 1992 against the Serbs it seems, but let's see what this reports about Mr. Pusic in 1993. Page 4: "When he became the head of the office for the exchange of prisoners of the HR HB, Pusic continued the same business. Pusic released over 100 MOS members from the military prison without the agreement of the SIS and the criminal department. "Pusic did this for money too." Your Honours, just a side note. It's interesting to note that Mr. Pusic is reported here as exerting his authority at will despite of what others authorities were supposed to do. It's without the agreement of SIS and the criminal department of the military police. Now, Your Honours this report concludes with the following: "We believe that throughout the war, Berislav Pusic has been working against the interests of the Croatian people and soldiers, and since the same can be expected in the future, we recommend that measures are taken so that Pusic be prevented from causing more damage to the reputation of the HVO." In the event, despite this report, nothing was done, and in August 1994, Pusic was still operating, as seen from Exhibit P08431 where he writes a long fax to the centre for human rights in which he spouts the manifestly false HVO version of the events in 1993 which the Trial Chamber has heard so often from various defence -- Defences in this case. It's a worthwhile read to see how zealously Pusic was still lying for his radical nationalist ideology. A sampling that I've selected is from 8431, page 3 -- or -- page 3. It says -- and here he's referring to Muslims who were captured in action. It says: "All prisoners stayed alive while Muslims were killing Croats and making mass graves." And on the same page: "The only prison which was registered was -- as a prison was Heliodrom, while Gabela and Dretelj were registered as collection centres which were known to the ICRC which was regularly visiting and resettling Muslims to third countries in accordance to their wish, and those who did not wish to go abroad, they crossed to the MOS-controlled side ..." Your Honours, the evidence before this court proves overwhelmingly that these were blatant lies. Many Muslims died in HVO detention. There were no "regular ICRC visits to Dretelj and Gabela," and the deportation of Muslim men from Dretelj and Gabela was not a question of Muslim detainees exercising a free choice at leisure. They were brutally expelled and deported against their wills by the likes of Mr. Berislav Pusic. To persuade the Court to accept his defence, Mr. Pusic must lie about his role and involvement. The evidence shows he's a man capable of doing exactly that. He is not an honest man. Now, Your Honours. If we can turn to Mr. Pusic and his power. May I ask at what time shall we take the break, until what time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, before the break, you have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, faced with the extensive evidence of his integral involvement with prisoner exchange and detainee issues, including forced labour, Mr. Pusic boldly asserts his innocence and the weakness of the Prosecution case. It's, however, nothing more than an impossible and preposterous story. Mr. Pusic simply ignores or speciously re-characterises the majority of the evidence against him, and he selectively takes snippets of testimony and evidence out of context in order to further his tenuous story-line that no one else in the HVO -- or that -- rather, I'll say that again. His story-line is that everyone else in the HVO around Mr. Pusic had the power. He himself possessed no power whatsoever, and his sole function was to maintain lists which were created and used by others. He then examined each piece of evidence in a vacuum to urge that the Prosecution's interpretation is not the only reasonable interpretation of that evidence. However, we submit when the evidence is examined outside the selective and myopic narrative presented by Mr. Pusic, when it is put into context of all the other evidence, as the Prosecution has done, then there is no doubt whatsoever. It's beyond any reasonable doubt that Mr. Pusic wielded the authority over prisoner detention and transfer and committed the crimes as alleged in the indictment. Aside from the specific orders assigning him to his various positions, some examples of his authority are, and if -- we have three slides: P02020 was an order from Mr. Coric on 22 April, 1993, and on page 2, he ordered: "Mr. Berko Pusic is charged with participating on behalf of the Military Police Administration in the exchange of all arrested persons." Your Honours, low-level administrative technicians are not given such authority. P02546. It's a 28 May 1993 report on the activities of the 4th brigade of the HVO military police, and on page 2 it says: "We received an order from Berko Pusic and Valentin Coric to transfer the prisoners to the prison on Heliodrom." The conclusion from this is if Pusic was so insignificant as he says, why would he have been mentioned at all? It would have been sufficient to say, "We received an order from Valentin Coric." P03652. This is a 23 July 1993 telex from Berislav Pusic to the HVO military police in Jablanica. And he says: "We would like to ask you to escort the Muslims you were given in our last -- we would like you to escort the Muslims you were given to our last check-point in Doljani from where they can walk to Jablanica. If they expel our Croats from Jablanica, inform us of it, because there will be a reaction against these men of theirs." Your Honours, these are not the words of an impotent filing clerk. Who were these Muslims referred to in this exhibit and whom Pusic requested that they be expelled under escort? And for this we can look at Exhibit P03668, also of 23 July 1993, and it's from the 3rd HVO battalion commander, and we see it's to Berislav Pusic personally in his capacity at the exchange commission and it says: These persons are 400 Muslim women, children, and elderly. They were brought to Doljani sector. "... please inform as soon as possible what we are to do with them and why they were sent to Doljani." We also see there's no food for these people. "Please instruct." Berislav Pusic was exerting his authority, and, Your Honours, his authority was recognised. In his final trial brief, Berislav Pusic asserts in paragraph 157 his "lack of decision-making authority is highlighted in a number of ECMM reports by their representatives attending prisoner exchange negotiations." In reference to a meeting chaired by the ICRC on 23 May, the ECMM representative notes Pusic advised those present he did not have the authority to sign the agreement reached on behalf of the HVO for access to the Heliodrom. He refers to Exhibit P02496 in that regard. Your Honours, however, the Pusic Defence in asserting this ignore Mr. Pusic's own direct words regarding his authority. On 19 October 1993, he was interviewed by Slobodna Dalmacija, and they published an interview with him in connection to talks about the exchange of detainees. This is Exhibit P05945. The title is "You reach an Agreement with Peter, Paul annuls it ..." He's interviewed as head of the office of the government of the HR HB for the exchange of captives. And on pages 4 and 5, the interviewer asks him: "Who are the people sitting opposite you during the talks you hold and what do you think of them as negotiators?" And Pusic, he says: "From the International Red Cross, there's Mr. Claudio Barancini ..." And then he says from the UN High Commission, it's Mr. Hulme. From the Spanish Battalion, Major Ferrero and Colonel Carvajal. And then he says: "From the Muslim side from the east side of Mostar, Messrs. Cakan Alispahic and Mr. Sevko Dziho, who have been very fair during the talks, come to the negotiations." And then he says: "But they are not the people who can decide. They must always go and get instructions from Mr. Arif Pasalic, who usually makes the final decision." And then he says when the subject of talks is Jablanica and Konjic, Mr. Zuka comes. And then he says, Your Honour: "Unlike the Croatian side," now, that's him, "unlike the Croatian side, the members of the commission they sent never had the power to decide. We formed the office attached to the HR of HB government which has all powers to make decisions on the issues of exchange and release of detainees while the Muslim side have some people to negotiate and others to decide." He says: "We have all the powers to make decision on the issues of exchange and release ..." Your Honour, further more, Mr. Pusic, he communicated directly with ministers of the Republic of Croatia reporting his own meeting with senior internationals, and in an ECMM document which we cannot show outside the court, Exhibit P05889, a report from 14 October 1993, he says it's reported: "Pusic head of the HVO office for the exchange of prisoners has sent a letter to Mate Granic, Croatian minister of foreign affairs. In the letter, Pusic informs Granic about his talks with Claudio Barancini, the head of the ICRC ..." Your Honour, Mr. Pusic was not a low-level rubber stamp. Hardly. These two exhibits, which show Mr. Pusic meeting with the head of the ICRC, also demolish Mr. Pusic's arguments found in paragraphs 174 and 75 of his brief that the Prosecution failed to distinguish between high-level and local prisoner exchange and release negotiations. According to Mr. Pusic, Mr. Pusic only participated in the low-level local negotiations and had no significant involvement in the high-level talks. Your Honour, I'm going to continue with this topic, but I think this is an appropriate place to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a break. You -- I would like to tell the Prosecution that so far they've used up 14 hours, so when we resume, you will have one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Kruger, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, before the break we were still addressing paragraph 174 and 175 of the Pusic final trial brief. That's the argument that the Prosecution has mischaracterised Pusic's role in the prisoner release and exchange process and that Mr. Pusic did not have any significant involvement in talks, also that he participated only in low-level, unimportant things. We had a look at Exhibits P05945 and P05889, and now I'd -- finally on this point, I wish to show another example. Mr. Pusic participated prominently in high-level negotiations with the ABiH in Jablanica in May 1993. Being present throughout the two-day process where they visited the school in Sovici and Doljani. He was with General Petkovic and others. Now, Mr. Pusic alleges in paragraph 233, 233 of his final trial brief, that his role was wholly insignificant. Your Honour, there are some visual images available on this meeting, and I'd like to refer to some. The first one is, and this comes from a video exhibit, P02187, and the first image that we see on the screen shows Mr. Pusic on the right of the screen sitting next to Miljenko Lasic and then General Milivoj Petkovic. They were part of a small specialist segment of the HVO delegation for this particular meeting. Who was sitting on the other side of the table, and if we can have a look at the next slide, we see that that is General Halilovic, and the next slide we see General Pasalic sitting there. And the question is: Was Mr. Pusic in this meeting only a seat warmer? And for this, I'd like to show a clip of Mr. Pusic's participation in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Today I would send them to Vrci and to other places where the wounded are so that they will be pulled out. We don't have to send ours from down there. I'm here now for the seventh time, and we still haven't broken the deadlock regarding the pulling out of the wounded and every time that was the goal. That's why I would propose now, together with SpaBat, that they do it. "That is a representative of the HVO and a representative of yours who has influence over those soldiers, and so let's go immediately and finish that today. "Yesterday you were wounded, you didn't want to go, the three from Kostajnica. "But the condition was the two dead. "Who set the condition? "Your man there in Vrce. "If you want, we can settle the issue of the dead right now. There are dead on both sides, yours and ours. "Do you think it's true? "Of course the information is true. "I don't think it could be done, but I don't see why they couldn't be collected immediately since a long time has elapsed from the day of death. The bodies start to decay, so collect the wounded and at the same time throw the dead ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Pusic participated in this meeting directly. He is seen responding forcefully to General Pasalic who is General Petkovic's ABiH counterpart, senior counterpart, and he does this while General Petkovic is sitting there right next to him. With respect, Your Honours, these were clearly high-level talks, and Pusic is significantly or was significantly involved. If we can look at another still from a video exhibit, and this is Exhibit P00999, and I'm not going to play the clip, but Mr. Pusic was interviewed by the Croatian media, and we see this was shown on HTV, Croatian television, and what is significant is how Mr. Pusic is identified. Even the Croatian media view him as somebody significant in the HVO. He is described as "HVO negotiator." Your Honour, if we can move on to a further topic, the question of whether Mr. Pusic was indeed only a rubber stamp in view of all the signed documents. There's a vast amount of documents with Mr. Pusic's signature. Mr. Pusic acknowledges his signature appeared on many documents regarding release, expulsion, and forced labour. He, of course, states these documents and his signature have no value because he was only a rubber stamp for authority exercised elsewhere. With respect, this is pure nonsense. Pusic's signature, as with anyone's meant something when he signed it. It meant that he claimed responsibility for a proposition, and in the case of his signature, that proposition was most frequently the authorisation to expel Muslims to third countries or to ABiH territory. His signature authorised the use of detainees for forced labour on a massive scale. His signature authorised the transfer and release of detainees. People sought Mr. Pusic's signature because he had power. That is why people present documents to other people to sign. Your Honour, Mr. Pusic makes much of the fact that others, witnesses -- sorry, that other people also at time exercised authority to release and exchange detainees. And this is from his final trial brief, page 58. The Prosecution case is not, as the Pusic Defence suggests in its final trial brief, that Mr. Pusic was the only one able to transfer prisoners, nor is it our case that he had the supreme control over every single aspect of detainee life and liberty. The evidence shows it was Pusic's mandated job to determine who would stay, who would go, and where they would go. When others ordered transfers and releases, it was incidental to their jobs or their positions. Mr. Pusic, however, exercised his authority throughout the HVO material in the course of the conflict from his involvement, and he consulted with the HVO leadership in making his decisions at times. As seen from P05889, he even consulted ministers from the Republic of Croatia on this. The Prosecution has never maintained that all of the blame for the criminal detention and expulsion scheme of the HVO falls at the feet of Berislav Pusic. However, the criminal activities of others does not absolve Mr. Pusic from his crimes when he wielded the power that he was given to further violate international law, rather than to abstain from doing so or pursuing those who were. Bruno Stojic, he placed the responsibility and power to release and exchange prisoners upon Mr. Pusic's shoulders when he set up the commission on 6 August 1993. And that's Exhibit P03995. Mr. Pusic exercised this responsibility throughout the rest of 1993. He often did this without following the outlined procedures, as we have seen, of engaging with the SIS and military police concurrence or involving other commission members. If we can have a look at Exhibit P04141. This is a 12 August 1993 decision by the commission, signed by Mr. Pusic, and it's in regard to the registration of detainees. And if we see the second paragraph it says: "Registration was carried out in Mostar, Ljubuski prison, and Otok, and detainees were classified." Of course we know this is false. That was never done. By December 1993, no classification had yet been done. He continues: "The release of prisoners from Dretelj and Gabela must be suspended for the purpose of the most expeditious registration possible and correct classification, and the commission will provide the above slips for ... registration ..." If we look at another exhibit, P06170. This is a 27 October 1993 memo by Josip Praljak on the work of the commission. And if we look at the bottom, it says: "As you are aware, the head of the prisoner exchange office, Mr. Pusic, can release these prisoners with the approval of the SIS and of the intelligence service of the military police ..." But then in the very next paragraph it says that: "Detainee Admir Cevra was being investigated by Mr. Misic, a SIS employee, who did not give his approval for release, but was then released on the basis of certain documents from Berislav Pusic." So Berislav Pusic did for the deem himself bound by the input of the SIS and the crime investigation department. He exerted his authority at will. Your Honours, Pusic was not the exclusive arbiter of the machinery of the HVO expulsion mechanism, but the evidence shows he selectively chose to act when it furthered the objectives of the JCE. His role was not routine ministerial list-keeping, which is uninteresting to him. And if we can look at P07102, on 10 December 1993. This is a proposal from Mr. Pusic to accused number 1, Mr. Prlic on the work of the service of exchange. On page 5 Mr. Pusic explains to Mr. Prlic: "The prisons are interesting for the service only for the purpose of seeking certain persons for exchange ..." Your Honours, it is not credible that someone who so explicitly indicated to someone no less than the head of government, Mr. Prlic, that he's not interested in prisoners except for the exchange -- from the exchange perspective. It's not credible that such a person would, in fact, only have been charged with simply keeping lists of prisoners for months on end. Your Honours, Mr. Pusic, he points in his final trial brief, to some instances where Mr. Pusic is not mentioned or is unknown to certain witnesses. This is the final trial brief of Mr. Pusic, on page 36. And this is stated as proof that he could not have played a leading role in the JCE. That certain evidence and testimony omits specific mention of Mr. Pusic does not negate all the other evidence of his involvement and participation in the JCE alleged. Witnesses who said nothing about Mr. Pusic's involvement were most likely in situations where they either did not have a Pusic-related basis of knowledge, or they did not have access to the internal processes and high-level discussions between Mr. Pusic and other members of the JCE. It doesn't mean, however, that such things did not take place. The same goes for his argument that he could not have been in the JCE because Slobodan Praljak did not know of him. And this is the Pusic final trial brief, paragraphs 14 and 15. This does for the remove the fact that he was known and interacted in the context of the JCE with the four other accused in the case, Messrs. Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Mr. Coric. The argument of not being in the JCE because he was unknown to some witnesses and an accused, it's an irrelevant red herring. Your Honours, certainly very few people inside and outside Nazi Germany knew of Adolph Eichmann and what exactly he was doing during 1942 and 1945. That does not negate the fact that he was the one who kept the trains running to transport Europe's Jews to the Nazi death camps and that he so participated in the Nazi genocide that was the Holocaust. It's irrelevant that some people did not know of Mr. Pusic or his exact role in 1993 in Herceg-Bosna. The evidence still abundantly shows Pusic was instrumental in the persecutory detention of thousands of Muslims in HVO detention facilities. Their persecutory utilisation for forced labour, and the ultimate persecutory, deportation, and expulsion of thousands of Muslims from the territory of the HZ-HB, or later HR HB. In conclusion, Your Honours, Mr. Pusic's allegations of being a lowly bureaucrat with no power at all is belied by his own end-of-year report in 1993. It's a report on the activities of the service for the exchange of prisoners and other persons of the HR HB, Exhibit P07411. On 31 December 1993, he reports, paragraph 1: "The service was founded as there was no central place to collect, process, and send back the information about the resolution of complex humanitarian problems in the process of exchange, but above all to facilitate the exchange of captives, missing, and dead." The next paragraph: "In the previous months, co-operation was established with the ICRC, UNPROFOR, European monitors, and other similar and related institutions in the area of HR HB and the Republic of Croatia." Regarding meetings held in the six months since being set up on 30 June, 1993, he reports in paragraph 3: "We held 18 meetings with representatives of Republika Srpska and 27 meetings with representatives of the RBH Army. The topics discussed were the exchange of detainees and dead and the evacuation of civilians. The service ... always tried to effect an exchange that would as favourable to our side as possible." Then he lists various statistics, numbers of exchanged people, dead people, and after listing these and all the release efforts, we come to paragraph 5: "The work of the Service Staff was mainly concerned with the detained Muslims." Then: "In co-operation with the office of displaced persons, SIS, and the crime investigation department of the Military Police Administration, it also effected the release from prison if detainees had completed documentation. The service did its part of the job fully." That says it all. This report apparently formulated in the words of Berislav Pusic, whose name appears as the author, shows the work Pusic was doing was indeed a cog in the HVO's machinery, but it was by no means disposable and insignificant. Pusic put the Prosecution to the proof of every allegation against him and responded with a passive and virtually silent defence. On the basis of this, Berislav Pusic argues that the evidence clearly shows Pusic was an MP officer who -- control officer who had nothing to control. He was the head of a prisoner exchange service who had neither the power over prisoners nor the power to exchange. He was appointed by the head of a government and the minister of defence and the head of the military police to do no more than be a stenographer. He was a custodian of records who introduced none of those records that he alleged he was charged with maintaining, but those people who did introduce his records into evidence he accuses of being self-serving liars. With respect, the evidence does not support Mr. Pusic's version, and the doubt that he asserts exists is not reasonable by any stretch of the imagination. The Prosecution submits, Your Honours, the evidence proves beyond any reasonable doubt his membership and participation in the JCE alleged, and his liability for the crimes he has been charged with as fully set out in the Prosecution's final trial brief. Mr. Pusic has shown no remorse for his misdeeds. He has shown no understanding for the suffering his actions have caused to the thousands of victims of his crimes, and the Prosecution submits that he should be sentenced -- convicted and sentenced as we have set out in our final trial brief. Your Honour, that concludes this section on Mr. Pusic, and if I can hand over to Mr. Scott again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Next. Good morning, Mr. Scott, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. This may be the last time that the Prosecution is on its feet in this case, so I would like to take a few moments to thank various persons in and around the courtroom before concluding the Prosecution's remarks. First, the Prosecution extends its sincere thanks to the translation booths for all the tremendous hard work over the many months. We likewise thank the court reporters for all of their work. We are very sorry for sometimes talking too fast and not always as clearly as one might wish. Despite the recent and current difficulties, we nonetheless thank the technicians for all of their support. Technology is a wonderful thing when it works, but may it never ever prevail over the human being. We thank the Registry for all of their hard work in trying to keep things straight. We thank the Chamber's legal officers for all the hard work that they have done and undoubtedly will do over the next months. We thank Your Honours for your attention and patience. The Prosecution never claimed that it would or could, or that has it has in fact presented a perfect case, but I can assure you without qualification that we have done our very best. We have never had any other agenda or desire except to present our case as effectively and efficiently as possible, to assist the Chamber in doing justice. We especially thank Judge Mindua for his long and faithful service as our alternate Judge. Finally, I take the luxury of this moment to thank the Prosecution team for all of their hard work and dedication, and especially Mr. Stringer, Ms. West, and Mr. Kruger for their terrific closing submissions. Thank you. Taken at face value, what the Defence arguments tell us is that either no one was responsible for anything, or if someone was responsible, it was certainly someone, anyone, other than the particular accused. On responsibility for the HVO camps, we see six men running as fast and far in the opposite direction as possible, or pointing the finger at one another. Prlic says that Boban and the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic's department, were responsible for the camps. Stojic says it was Boban, HVO military commanders, HVO municipal authorities and ODPR, part of Mr. Prlic's government, who were responsible. Praljak says it was the civilian HVO government, that is Mr. Prlic's HVO HZ-HB, that was responsible for the camps. In his sworn testimony, Petkovic said it was the Stojic Defence Department which was responsible, and in his final brief, he's added that the Military Police Administration was also responsible. Coric says it was individual HVO military unit commanders who were responsible for all of the persons which that unit detained. And Pusic says, concerning the Muslim men arrested after 30 June 1993, that it was the military police who were responsible for processing them. So where do all these Defence claims leave us? With respect, Your Honours, a government president, an intelligent, obviously capable man who climbed to the pinnacles of power and then claimed he had none. A man who was the head of this and the top of that, a man who based his entire course on power, position, and influence, but now says that his only job was to send out notices of meetings and sign decisions made by others. A head of the Defence Department who Petkovic referred to as "his minister," who Petkovic expressly placed in his chain of command, who Susak reported to Tudjman was "organising everything down there," a man who most others say was in charge of the HVO camps, but who, according to Stojic himself, was doing nothing more than ordering cap badges and sitting in on a few meetings. Two generals, one a theatre director and one a professional soldier, both of whom say that all they wanted was social harmony but who presided over an army and participated in making and executing policy that wreaked ethnic violence and havoc in tens of thousands of lives, by officers and soldiers who they say they controlled. They blame the politicians, and the politicians blame them. Sadly, the Prosecution submits that the HVO commanders and soldiers only did what they were explicitly or implicitly told and encouraged to do. A chief of military police who organised training programmes for his subordinates on the laws of war which many of them thereafter breached with impunity on an almost daily basis. Despite his self-described role as a minor administrator, he inexplicably rose on Tudjman's personal endorsement to Herceg-Bosna's minister of interior. The head of a refugee and exchange service who always had the best interests of Muslims in mind and for whom he generously provided a one-way bus service out of Herceg-Bosna. President John Kennedy said in a speech at American University in June 1963: "World peace, like community, does not require that each man love his neighbour - it requires only that they live together in mutual tolerance, submitting their disputes to a just and peaceful settlement ... Peace need not be impracticable, and war need not be inevitable. For in the final analysis, our most basic common link as human beings is that we all inhabit this small planet. We all breathe the same air. We all cherish our children's future. And we are all mortal." It seems to me, Your Honours, that some people forgot that, but we cannot let them forget that, or the ones who might come next, or the ones who might come after that. Mankind has a problem - after every round of horrible massive violence, we say "Never again." We cannot forget this. We will not forget this. "We cannot let them forget this," and by saying "them," we mean the next ones, the next ones who might be tempted to do the same thing. We cannot let them forget that. But we do. We do. We do forget. Never again, until the next time, and the next time. The Holocaust, Cambodia, Yugoslavia, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Darfur. Can I stop the next time? Can you? Maybe, maybe not. This is your best chance, Your Honours, President Antonetti, Judge Prandler, Judge Trechsel, Judge Mindua, this is your best chance to say, "Never again," and really mean it. We won't stand for this. We won't stand for this. We couldn't stop, we didn't stop the last one, but we can hold these men accountable. You've heard the accused. Do you remember the victims? Over the past four and a half years you've seen and heard the accused often, almost daily. You've heard their voices repeatedly. We all probably remember Mr. Stojic standing up one day in court and telling the courtroom about a grandchild being born. As I've sat here these past months, I've often wondered what it might have been like if throughout the trial we had had six representative victims sitting behind the Prosecution, just as the accused sit behind Defence counsel. Maybe one of them would have stood up one day and said, "Maybe I would be a grandmother today if my daughter had not been killed in Mostar," or, "Today would have been my son's 37th birthday if he had not died in a HVO camp." Do you remember the victims? Do you hear their voices? In a former life I prosecuted a lot of financial crime, what some call white-collar crime. I confess I was always disappointed to encounter some Judges who for some reason were only too happy to send the young black man to prison for stealing a loaf of bread or $50 worth of gasoline, but somehow didn't feel the same way when there was someone who looked like a businessman in front of them, wearing a suit and looking awfully, quote, "normal," but who by the stroke of a pen had embezzled or defrauded someone of a million dollars. The thought being, well, that man, that guy looks pretty much like us. He wears a suit. He looks like someone who goes to church on Sundays. In fact, he looks a lot like the accused here. The Security Council mandate is not for the ICTY to prosecute all the men who pulled the triggers or lit the matches but to hold accountable those who were most responsible, who caused these things to happen at a much higher level. Since at least a Security Council statement in 2002, the Tribunal has been repeatedly urged to concentrate its work, quote, "on the prosecution and trial of the most senior leaders suspected of being responsible for crimes within the [Tribunal's] jurisdiction ..." But I wonder whether it is often not easier to impose a heavy sentence on someone like the thug Goran Jelisic, who was sentenced to 40 years' imprisonment because he repeatedly personally pulled the trigger in executing a number of non-Serb prisoners held at the Serbs' Luka camp in 1992 than on the senior civilian and military leaders who put people like Jelisic in the very situation in which hundreds or thousands of such horrific crimes were committed. The concept or phrase "the banality of evil," came into prominence from the 1963 book by Hannah Arendt, "Eichmann in Jerusalem, A Report on the Banality of Evil," in which among other things she commented on how this rather ordinary or normal looking person, at least by outward appearance, could have been involved in carrying out the most unspeakable crimes. But as Mr. Kruger reminded us today, Eichmann was a top administrator in the machinery of the Nazi camps. I'm sure he never personally put anyone to death, he never personally lit an oven, never personally did those things, probably, but he ran the machinery who accepted the policies and premises of his state and participated in the ongoing evil with the energy and diligence and dedication of a good bureaucrat. The German playwright and novelist Goethe said: "Behaviour is a mirror in which everyone displays his own image." In this regard, and as Mr. Stringer mentioned today, the accused may point to a few instances where an HVO soldier was punished for a crime against a Muslim civilian. We submit that there is no evidence of very much of that, but perhaps, probably, there were a few. Let me set out the situation this way: Imagine a train taking a carload or carloads of prisoners to a Nazi death camp. During the time on the train, a Nazi guard steals a watch and takes jewellery from a Jewish woman on the train. As circumstances would have it, a top German officer comes by, finds out about the situation and punishes the German soldier for stealing the watch and taking the jewellery. But he didn't stop the train. The train continues on to the final destination, the final solution. I say to you concerning these accused, they might have looked like church-goers on Sunday, but when they were doing what they did, when they were establishing, promoting, instigating, ordering, and supporting ethnic cleansing, they were thugs. They were thugs. No better than Goran Jelisic who pulled the trigger himself. For Jadranko Prlic, the Prosecution asks for a sentence of 40 years. For Bruno Stojic, the Prosecution asks for a sentence of 40 years. For Slobodan Praljak, the Prosecution asks for a sentence of 40 years. For Milivoj Petkovic, the Prosecution asks for a sentence of 40 years. For Valentin Coric, the Prosecution asks for a sentence of 35 years. For Berislav Pusic, the Prosecution asks for a sentence of 25 years. Do you hear the voices, Your Honours? Do you hear the voices, the voices of the victims? Sometimes often the voices start as whispers, whispers for lots of reasons, whispers because some are still embarrassed or ashamed about what happened; whispers because some don't want to relive the horrible things ever again, not even to say the words out loud; whispers because they've given up being heard, because no one seems to listen to them anyway; whispers because they feel powerless. But then many of the voices become more than whispers. The voices grow louder. You hear them from Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica and Mostar and Stolac, from the Heliodrom, from Dretelj, from Gabela, from Ljubuski. And they are not all Muslim voices. There are Croat voices, too, from Croat victims. Not the victims of the Serbs, not the victims of the Muslims - and there were - but the victims, the Croat victims of Greater Croatia, because of the nationalist ambitions of these men and others around them, these Croat victims lost loved ones. These Croat victims lost their homes. These Croat victims lost their livelihood. They were victims too. Do you hear the voices? Judges, do you hear the voices? We hold a certain power as stewards for the powerless, for the victims, to do justice. Let me say that again. We hold a certain power as stewards for the powerless, for the victims, to do justice. We must, as stewards act on their behalf in seeking justice, in doing justice, to empower the powerless. Do you remember the victims? Do you hear their voices? The Muslim women and children in Prozor may have been powerless in October 1992 to prevent themselves from being expelled from their homes, but not today. The Muslim villagers who had their mosque destroyed in Sovici in April 1993 might have been powerless to stop it, but not today. The Muslim families who were kicked out of their homes in the Dum neighbourhood in West Mostar on the 14th of June, 1993, might have been powerless to stop it, but not today. The elderly Muslim couple cowering with a single candle in a Mostar basement hiding from HVO shelling might have been powerless to stop it, but not today. Witness BQ on being released from Dretelj might have been almost powerless to walk from Vrda to Dreznica, but not today. Mufida Likic may have been powerless to stop the HVO soldiers from murdering her sister, her aunt, and her neighbour in that potato cellar in Stupni Do, but not today. Do you hear the voices? They cry for justice.
